executive_summary.heading: Overview
paragraphs: Thapar Institute of Engineering and Technology commissioned a secure source code review of KavachBank. The review was performed on 12 November 2026 with CodeKavach, combining deterministic rule and taint analysis with model-assisted triage under a privacy-preserving egress policy. 29 files and 936 lines of YAML, Python, JavaScript, Dockerfile, Terraform code were analysed.

The review identified 59 findings (15 critical, 27 high, 12 medium, 5 low). The overall security posture is rated critical: at least one weakness can be exploited to compromise the application or its data, and immediate action is required. 6 findings are supported by a complete source-to-sink data-flow trace. 12 findings were independently assessed by the language model gpt-5.6-sol (agentrouter); it judged 5 of them exploitable. Model assessments are advisory and no finding was dismissed by a model.

executive_summary.heading: Most significant findings
bullets: CK-2026-001 (Critical): A pull_request_target workflow checks out the pull request head, running untrusted code with repository secrets and a write token. An attacker can run code with the pipeline's secrets and write token, tamper with releases and pivot into the supply chain.
CK-2026-002 (Critical): Container 'api' is privileged. Any other weakness in the component becomes a full host or cluster compromise, because the attacker inherits the excess privileges.

CK-2026-003 (Critical): Data from a http_param source reaches a sql sink (cur.execute). If account_id is attacker-controlled, an attacker can alter the SELECT query and potentially cause find_premium_account to return unauthorized database rows; broader effects depend on the database driver and account permissions.

CK-2026-004 (Critical): Hard-coded credential of type connection_string (masked preview po****** (51 chars), entropy 4.91 bits/char). Anyone with access to the repository, a build artefact or a decompiled binary obtains the credential; rotating it requires a code change and redeployment.

CK-2026-005 (Critical): Hard-coded credential of type aws_access_key (masked preview AK****** (20 chars), entropy 3.68 bits/char). Anyone with access to the repository, a build artefact or a decompiled binary obtains the credential; rotating it requires a code change and redeployment.

executive_summary.heading: Where the weaknesses concentrate
paragraphs: The most frequent weakness classes are CWE-798 Use of Hard-coded Credentials (11); CWE-250 Execution with Unnecessary Privileges (8); CWE-1395 Dependency on Vulnerable Third-Party Component (8). By OWASP Top 10 category the largest group is A07:2021 Identification and Authentication Failures (12 findings). Recurring classes indicate a missing shared control rather than isolated mistakes, so the recommendations below address the control as well as each instance.

executive_summary.heading: Strategic recommendations
bullets: Immediate (within 7 days): Revoke and rotate the exposed credential immediately, then load it at run time from a secret manager or environment. [CK-2026-004, CK-2026-005, CK-2026-006, CK-2026-007 and others]
Immediate (within 7 days): Upgrade the component to a fixed version, or remove it if it is not needed. [CK-2026-015]
Short term (within 30 days): Upgrade the component to a fixed version, or remove it if it is not needed. [CK-2026-026, CK-2026-027, CK-2026-038, CK-2026-040 and others]
Short term (within 30 days): Run the component as a non-root user, drop the privileged flag and grant only the capabilities it needs. [CK-2026-018, CK-2026-019, CK-2026-021, CK-2026-022]
Medium term (within 90 days): Run the component as a non-root user, drop the privileged flag and grant only the capabilities it needs. [CK-2026-043, CK-2026-044, CK-2026-047]
Medium term (within 90 days): Encode output for its HTML context (or use a template engine with auto-escaping) and never send raw request data with res.send or equivalent. [CK-2026-051, CK-2026-054]
Planned (next release cycle): Do not check out untrusted code in privileged workflows; pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA and reduce the token permissions. [CK-2026-058, CK-2026-059]
Planned (next release cycle): Pin the component to a reviewed version or digest and replace unmaintained components. [CK-2026-055, CK-2026-057]
Embed the deterministic rules in CI so that the weakness classes found here are blocked at pull-request time, and schedule a retest once the fixes are deployed.

roadmap.action: Revoke and rotate the exposed credential immediately, then load it at run time from a secret manager or environment.
Upgrade the component to a fixed version, or remove it if it is not needed.

roadmap.theme: Inclusion of Functionality from Untrusted Control Sphere
roadmap.action: Do not check out untrusted code in privileged workflows; pin third-party actions to a full commit SHA and reduce the token permissions.
Stop passing the command to a shell: call the program with an argument list (shell=False) and validate each argument against a strict allow-list.
Use parameterised queries or prepared statements for every value that reaches the query; never format user data into SQL text.
Upgrade the component to a fixed version, or remove it if it is not needed.
Run the component as a non-root user, drop the privileged flag and grant only the capabilities it needs.
Scope every lookup to the authenticated principal (for example WHERE owner_id = current_user) and return 404 for records the caller does not own.
Resolve the final path and reject it unless it lies inside an allow-listed base directory; prefer opaque identifiers mapped server-side to file names.
Revoke and rotate the exposed credential immediately, then load it at run time from a secret manager or environment.

roadmap.theme: Exposure of Resource to Wrong Sphere
roadmap.action: Restrict the exposure to the intended network or principals.
Re-enable certificate and hostname verification.
Use at least 2048-bit RSA or 256-bit elliptic curves and AES-128 or stronger.

roadmap.theme: Incorrect Permission Assignment for Critical Resource
roadmap.action: Tighten the permissions to the owning principal only.
Add the authentication and authorisation guard used elsewhere in the service to this route, defaulting to deny.
Stop passing the command to a shell: call the program with an argument list (shell=False) and validate each argument against a strict allow-list.
Generate a fresh random IV (or nonce) for every encryption with a CSPRNG and store it alongside the ciphertext.
Add the missing access check, denying by default.
Validate the destination against an allow-list of hosts and schemes and block private, loopback and link-local address ranges after DNS resolution.

roadmap.theme: Use of a Broken or Risky Cryptographic Algorithm
roadmap.action: Hash passwords with a slow, salted, memory-hard function such as Argon2id, scrypt or bcrypt, and migrate existing hashes on next login.
Run the component as a non-root user, drop the privileged flag and grant only the capabilities it needs.
Encode output for its HTML context (or use a template engine with auto-escaping) and never send raw request data with res.send or equivalent.

Disable debug mode and remove debug endpoints from production builds.
Upgrade the component to a fixed version, or remove it if it is not needed.

findings.likelihood_rationale: OWASP likelihood high; confirmed source-to-sink path

lines.text: cur.execute("SELECT * FROM premium_accounts WHERE id = '%s'" % account_id)

verdict.reasoning: Line 6 is a security-relevant SQL sink: Python percent-formatting embeds account_id into the statement before cursor.execute receives it, so database parameter binding or escaping is not applied. There are no conditional guards between function entry and the sink, making the path satisfiable whenever cursor creation succeeds. Quoting '%s' is not a sanitizer because input containing a quote can change the SQL structure. However, this slice only establishes account_id as a function argument and does not independently prove that an attacker can control it; the rule name alone is insufficient to establish that source.

findings.description: Data from a http_param source reaches a sql sink (cur.execute). A database query is built by concatenating or interpolating data that an external party controls, so that data is parsed as SQL rather than treated as a value.
findings.impact: If account_id is attacker-controlled, an attacker can alter the SELECT query and potentially cause find_premium_account to return unauthorized database rows; broader effects depend on the database driver and account permissions.
findings.remediation_short_term: If account_id can be attacker-controlled, use the database driver's parameter-binding API and pass account_id separately from the SQL text, without quoting the placeholder. Optionally enforce the expected identifier type as defense in depth.
findings.remediation_long_term: Standardise on an ORM or query builder that parameterises by default, restrict the database account to the least privilege required, and add query-construction checks to code review and CI.
references: CWE-89: Improper Neutralization of Special Elements used in an SQL Command ('SQL Injection')

verdict.reasoning: This is a hardcoded-credential exposure rather than an attacker-input sink. razorpayKeyId contains the hardcoded razorpay key id and razorpayKeySecret contains the corresponding the hardcoded razorpay key secret. Both values are unconditionally placed in module.exports when the module loads, so the path is satisfiable and consumers of the module can access them. No sanitization or indirection protects the credentials; possession of the source or deployed artifact reveals the credential pair.

findings.description: Hard-coded credential of type razorpay_key_id (masked preview rz****** (23 chars), entropy 4.26 bits/char). A credential such as a password, API key or token is embedded in the source code.
findings.impact:
Exposure of an active production pair can compromise the associated merchant API identity. An attacker may access payment and customer transaction metadata and perform unauthorized payment operations allowed by the account, potentially causing privacy breaches, fraudulent activity, refunds, or financial loss. If the credentials are test-only, expired, or revoked, the practical impact is substantially reduced.

Attack scenario: An attacker gains read access to a source repository, packaged application, container image, backup, or deployed server and extracts `razorpayKeyId` and `razorpayKeySecret`. They then use the pair to authenticate directly to Razorpay, enumerate payment or order records, and invoke authorized operations such as creating payment resources, capturing payments, or issuing refunds, depending on the account's enabled APIs and permissions.

Affected: The Razorpay merchant account associated with the embedded credential pair; Payment, order, refund, and related customer transaction data accessible through the Razorpay API; Integrity of payment operations authorized for the account, including captures or refunds where permitted

Preconditions: The embedded credentials must still be valid and associated with a usable Razorpay account. The attacker must obtain read access to the source or an artifact containing this module and be able to reach the Razorpay API. Financial and production-data impact additionally requires these to be production rather than test credentials and for the relevant API operations to be enabled.
findings.remediation_short_term:
1. Revoke and rotate the exposed credential pair immediately.
2. Store the replacement values in the deployment platform's secrets manager; use protected environment variables only if a secrets manager is unavailable.
3. Replace the hardcoded values in razorpayKeyId and razorpayKeySecret with runtime secret lookups.
4. Validate both values at startup and fail closed when either is absent; do not add hardcoded fallback values.
5. Remove the credentials from repository history, build caches, published packages, and deployment artifacts after rotation.
6. Update each deployment environment with its own replacement credentials and verify authentication succeeds.

Secure example:
```javascript
razorpayKeyId: process.env.razorpayKeyId,
  razorpayKeySecret: process.env.razorpayKeySecret,
```

Defence in depth:
- Enable secret scanning in pre-commit hooks and CI to block future committed credentials.
- Use separate, least-privileged credentials for each environment and rotate them periodically.
- Prevent configuration objects and environment contents from being exposed through logs, diagnostics, or error responses.
findings.remediation_long_term: Adopt a secret manager, add pre-commit and CI secret scanning, and purge the value from version-control history.

lines.text: """Pack a folder of statements into an archive for download."""

verdict.reasoning: At line 7, archive_name and folder are interpolated directly into a command string passed to subprocess.run with shell=True. The path from the function parameters to the sink is direct and unconditional, so shell metacharacters supplied in either value can reach the shell. findings.description: A shell command is built from variable parts that are not quoted. The application builds an operating-system command from data that an external party can influence and runs it through a shell. Shell metacharacters in that data change the command that is executed.
findings.impact:
An attacker can execute arbitrary operating-system commands as the application account. This can expose readable data and credentials, modify or delete accessible files, compromise application integrity, and interrupt service. Broader host or connected-system compromise is possible if the process has elevated privileges or valuable credentials.

Attack scenario: An attacker supplies a crafted value for `archive_name` containing a command separator followed by an operating-system command. When the application calls `archive_statements`, the shell interprets the injected text as an additional command rather than as a literal `zip` argument. The injected command can then read files, alter application data, or disrupt the host within the process account's permissions.

Affected: Files and data accessible to the application process; Application host integrity and availability; Secrets and credentials available to the process

Preconditions: An attacker must be able to influence `archive_name` or `folder` and cause `archive_statements` to run. A command shell must be available, as expected by `shell=True`. The resulting access is limited by the operating-system privileges, filesystem access, credentials, and network reachability of the application process.
findings.remediation_short_term:
1. Replace the formatted command string with an argument list.
2. Remove `shell=True`; `subprocess.run` then invokes the program without shell interpretation.
3. Validate `archive_name` and `folder` against the narrow syntax required by the application, especially to prevent command-line option injection.
4. Keep `check=True` so execution failures are not silently ignored.

Secure example:
```python
subprocess.run(["zip", "-x", archive_name, folder], check=True)
```

Defence in depth:
- Allow-list each parameter according to its expected filename or pattern grammar, including rejecting unexpected option-like values such as those beginning with `-`.
- Run the process with minimal filesystem permissions and access only to the required files.
- Use a trusted executable path or tightly controlled `PATH`, and consider a timeout to constrain subprocess execution.
findings.remediation_long_term: Replace shell invocations with native library calls where possible, run the service with least privilege, and add a static-analysis gate that blocks shell=True and string-built commands.

verdict.reasoning: The request-derived req.query.file flows directly into path.join and then to the security-relevant fs.createReadStream sink. The path is unconditional, and an input containing sufficient ../ components can normalize outside config.exportDir. path.join only normalizes the path; it does not validate that the result remains under config.exportDir. No effective allowlist, canonical containment check, or other path-traversal defense is present.

findings.description: Data from a http_param source reaches a path sink (fs.createReadStream). A file-system path is built from data an external party controls without checking that the resolved path stays inside the intended directory.
findings.impact:
An attacker can make the application read files outside the intended directory and, where the stream is returned to the requester, obtain any such file readable by the service account. This can disclose application secrets, credentials, source code, or host/container configuration and enable follow-on compromise of associated systems.

Attack scenario: An attacker requests the handler with `file` set to a traversal value such as `../../../../etc/passwd` or a path targeting an application configuration file. After query decoding and path normalization, `fs.createReadStream` opens the file outside `config.exportDir`, and the handler streams its contents through `pipe(res)`, potentially revealing credentials or other sensitive data.

Affected: Files readable by the server process outside `config.exportDir`, including configuration, source code, credentials, and other sensitive local data; Accounts or downstream services whose credentials are stored in readable files

Preconditions: The attacker must be able to invoke `exportStatement` and control `req.query.file`; traversal sequences must reach the handler without effective upstream validation; and the target file must exist and be readable by the server process. Direct disclosure also requires `pipe(res)` to expose the stream to the requester, as is typical for a file-serving response path.
findings.remediation_short_term: Prefer mapping an allowlisted identifier to a server-controlled filename. Otherwise, canonicalize both config.exportDir and the requested file, reject absolute or traversal paths, verify the canonical result remains beneath the canonical base directory, and account for symlink escapes.
findings.remediation_long_term: Centralise file access behind a storage service that enforces containment, and run the process with a file-system view restricted to the data it needs.
references: CWE-22: Improper Limitation of a Pathname to a Restricted Directory ('Path Traversal')

verdict.reasoning: The HTTP-controlled value `req.query.file` reaches the filesystem path used by `fs.createReadStream`, so the sink is security-relevant. However, `path.resolve(root, req.query.file)` normalizes absolute paths and `..` components, and the subsequent separator-aware prefix check permits the sink only when the normalized path is strictly beneath `root`. Attempts to resolve outside the base, including sibling-prefix paths, take the rejecting branch and return. Thus the path to the sink is satisfiable only for contained paths, and the validation is effective against direct path traversal. This check would not prevent traversal through an attacker-controlled symbolic link already beneath `root`, but no ability to create or control such a link is shown.

findings.description: Data from a http_param source reaches a path sink (fs.createReadStream). A file-system path is built from data an external party controls without checking that the resolved path stays inside the intended directory.
findings.impact: An attacker can read or overwrite files outside the intended directory, including configuration files, credentials and other customers' documents.
findings.remediation_short_term: Do not use request data as a file path. findings.likelihood_rationale: OWASP likelihood high; entry point network; confirmed source-to-sink path

verdict.reasoning: At line 4, attacker-influenced data from req.query.name is concatenated directly into an HTML-shaped string passed to res.send. The sink is security-relevant because send commonly emits a string response as HTML. The path is unconditional once renderGreeting is invoked, and no validation, contextual HTML encoding, or other sanitizer occurs before the value reaches the sink. An attacker can therefore supply markup or script through name and have it interpreted by the browser.

findings.description: Data from a http_param source reaches a html sink (res.send). Data from the request is written into an HTML response without context-aware output encoding, so a browser may interpret it as markup or script.
findings.impact:
An attacker can execute JavaScript in another user's browser under the application's origin. This can expose same-origin page data and non-HttpOnly credentials or tokens, alter displayed content, and perform application actions using the victim's authenticated session. The code shown supports reflected rather than persistent exploitation.

Attack scenario: An attacker creates a URL whose `name` query value contains markup that breaks out of the surrounding element and executes JavaScript. The attacker sends the URL to an authenticated user. When the user opens it, `renderGreeting` reflects the payload in the HTML response, and the browser executes it under the application's origin, allowing the payload to read same-origin data and issue authenticated requests as the victim.

Affected: Browser data accessible to scripts under the application's origin; Authenticated user actions and application data available through the victim's session; Integrity of content displayed to the victim

Preconditions: `renderGreeting` must be reachable through an HTTP request; the attacker must control `name`; `res.send` must return the constructed string as browser-rendered HTML; and no downstream sanitizer or effective browser policy such as a restrictive CSP may prevent execution. A victim must load the crafted request.
findings.remediation_short_term:
1. Use a maintained HTML-encoding library such as `escape-html`.
2. Convert the query value to a string and encode it immediately before insertion into the HTML response.
3. Keep the encoded value in HTML text content; use the encoder appropriate to the destination if it is later moved into an attribute, URL, script, or style context.
4. If markup is not required, remove the HTML wrapper and explicitly send a `text/plain` response instead.
5. Add regression tests using angle brackets, quotes, entities, and event-handler markup.

Secure example:
```javascript
res.send(
  '<xx>xxxxxxx xxxx, ' +
  require('escape-html')(String(req.query.name ?? '')) +
  '</xx>'
);
```

Defence in depth:
- Deploy a restrictive Content Security Policy, preferably without `unsafe-inline`, to reduce impact if another injection path exists.
- Apply business-specific type and length limits to `req.query.name`; do not treat validation as a substitute for output encoding.
- Prefer an auto-escaping server-side template engine for responses containing multiple dynamic HTML values.
findings.remediation_long_term: Adopt auto-escaping templates throughout, deploy a strict Content-Security-Policy, and set HttpOnly on session cookies.
references: CWE-79: Improper Neutralization of Input During Web Page Generation ('Cross-site Scripting')

The zero-leak check is verbatim: it looks for the listed terms as written and does not detect a term that was paraphrased, split or encoded. The structure of the code, its control flow, the libraries it uses and the technology stack are still disclosed to the model whatever the privacy level.
